Article.ArticleTitle: 161 Patient-Reported Outcomes After Epidural Steroid Injections vs Surgery for Degenerative Lumbar Disease: A Prospective, Matched Cohort Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Despite the widespread use of surgery for degenerative lumbar disease (DLD), the comparative effectiveness of surgery vs epidural steroid injections (ESIs) is not well established. A few studies have compared surgery with medical/interventional treatments; however, they (1) do not specify what constitutes nonoperative care, (2) focus only on 1 diagnosis, or (3) do not use standardized outcome measures. Here we present a prospective, matched cohort study designed specifically to compare patient-reported outcomes (PRO) after ESI vs surgery for DLD.

Over 4 years, every patient at our institution who underwent elective lumbar surgery was enrolled in a prospective registry. Each week, patients who were surgical candidates but opted for conservative management were randomly enrolled into a separate registry. These registries were used to track PROs after 3 and 12 months. Univariate linear regression was conducted to determine what preoperative variables are associated with PROs, and this formed the basis for one-to-one matching across the 2 cohorts. Two-sample t tests were then performed to compare various PROs between the matched cohorts.

A total of 1701 surgical patients and 230 ESI patients were enrolled with 12-month follow-up, and matching yielded 82 patients in each group. Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), EQ-5D (quality of life), back pain, and leg pain scores were significantly better for the surgical group at 3 months (P = .001-.05), and all scores apart from ODI continued to be superior at 12 months (P = .001-.02). The degree of improvement was also greater in the surgical group for each PRO at 3 months (P = .003-.05), whereas at 12 months, this only held true for back and leg pain (P = .004-.005).

Across multiple degenerative lumbar pathologies, surgery is superior to ESI for improving quality of life and pain. This difference does not hold for disability level (ODI) 1 year after treatment, however.
